\chapter{Theatre, Exhibition, Circus}
\label{ch:teatro-exposicion-circo}
\hlchaptermodality{420}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the theatre, an exhibition and the circus, and say what each word is actually named after: the audience, a putting-out, and the shape of the floor.}

Propose an outing to each of the five places, choosing al or a la without stopping to think, because the -cion ending already told you which one is feminine.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el teatro]{el teatro — a place for looking, and the word theory came from it}

\label{lesson:ES-C420-teatro}



\begin{quote}
You can already name \emph{el cine}. Say it, then say the building people went to for two thousand years before there was any such thing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el cine — the other place you go to watch something, and the one whose name is barely a century old.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{stress-penultimate} — \emph{te-A-tro}, stress on the second of three. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — the \textbf{r} is one flick of the tongue, not a growl.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el teatro} — \textquotedblleft{}the theatre.\textquotedblright{} Latin \emph{theatrum}, from Greek \textbf{théatron}, \textquotedblleft{}a place for viewing,\textquotedblright{} built on \emph{theáomai}, \textquotedblleft{}to behold.\textquotedblright{}

The Greeks named the building after \textbf{what the audience does}, not after what happens on the stage. A theatre is a looking-place.

Now the payoff. That same \emph{theá-} gives Greek \emph{theōría} — \textquotedblleft{}a viewing, a contemplation\textquotedblright{} — which arrives in English as \textbf{theory}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{theat}re, amphi\textbf{theat}re — the looking-place.
  \item \textbf{theor}y, \textbf{theor}etical — what you see when you look hard at something.
\end{itemize}

A theory and a theatre are the same idea twice: \textbf{someone standing back and watching.} Spanish keeps both, \emph{teatro} and \emph{teoría}, and they have never stopped being cousins.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two names, two ages}]
Set the two buildings beside each other:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{place} & \textbf{named after} & \textbf{age of the word} \\
\midrule
el teatro & what the audience does — viewing & ancient Greek \\
el cine & what the machine does — writing movement & about 1900 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both are masculine and both take \emph{el}. One is among the oldest words in this book and one is among the newest, and you learned them a chapter apart.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el teatro\textquotedblright{} — \emph{te-A-tro}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el cine y el teatro\textquotedblright{} — both places, both masculine
  \item which English word for an idea comes from the same root as \emph{teatro} (theory)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did the Greeks name the theatre after — the stage, or the audience? (The audience: \emph{théatron} is a place for viewing.) What everyday English word for an explanation shares that root? (\emph{Theory}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la exposición]{la exposición — a putting-out}

\label{lesson:ES-C420-exposicion}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{el museo}. A museum holds its collection all year. Say the word for the thing a museum puts on for three months and then takes down.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el museo — the building. This lesson is the event inside it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{accent-acute} — the accent is on the last syllable: \emph{ex-po-si-CIÓN}. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{ci-th-s} — the \textbf{c} before \textbf{i} is the soft one.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la exposición} — \textquotedblleft{}the exhibition.\textquotedblright{} Latin \emph{expositio}: \textbf{ex-} (\textquotedblleft{}out\textquotedblright{}) plus \textbf{ponere} (\textquotedblleft{}to place\textquotedblright{}). An exhibition is literally \textbf{a putting-out}.

\emph{ponere} is one of the most productive verbs Latin ever handed on. Once you see it, it is everywhere:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ex\textbf{pos}e, ex\textbf{pos}ition — placed out.
  \item com\textbf{pos}e — placed together. de\textbf{pos}it — placed down.
  \item \textbf{pos}ition, post\textbf{pone}, com\textbf{pon}ent, op\textbf{pon}ent.
\end{itemize}

Spanish has the verb itself, \emph{poner}, \textquotedblleft{}to put\textquotedblright{} — so \emph{exposición} is transparent to a Spanish speaker in a way that \emph{exhibition} is not to an English one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending that tells you the gender}]
\begin{quote}
Nouns ending in \textbf{-ción} are feminine, without exception worth worrying about.
\end{quote}

\emph{la exposición}, \emph{la habitación}, \emph{la nación}. The ending comes from Latin \emph{-tio}, which was feminine, and Spanish kept the gender along with the sound.

That makes \textbf{-ción} one of the few endings you can trust on sight — most noun gender has to be learned with the word, and this one does not.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}la exposición\textquotedblright{} — accent on the last syllable
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el museo y la exposición\textquotedblright{} — the building and the event
  \item which article a noun ending in \emph{-ción} takes, and why (\emph{la} — the ending is feminine, from Latin \emph{-tio})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two Latin pieces inside \emph{exposición}, and what do they add up to? (\emph{ex-} \textquotedblleft{}out\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{ponere} \textquotedblleft{}to place\textquotedblright{} — a putting-out.) What gender does \textbf{-ción} guarantee? (Feminine.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el circo]{el circo — the ring, and the two c's in one word}

\label{lesson:ES-C420-circo}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Circo} has two \textbf{c}'s and they are not the same sound. Before reading on, say the word and listen to which one is soft.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ci-th-s} — the first \textbf{c}, before \textbf{i}, is soft. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{c-hard} — the second \textbf{c}, before \textbf{o}, is hard, as in \emph{cat}.
  \item \texttt{stress-penultimate} — \emph{CIR-co}.
\end{itemize}

One word, one letter, two jobs. The vowel that follows decides, every time.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el circo} — \textquotedblleft{}the circus.\textquotedblright{} Latin \emph{circus}, \textquotedblleft{}a ring,\textquotedblright{} borrowed from Greek \emph{kírkos}. The Romans' \emph{Circus Maximus} was a ring you raced around; the tent came much later and kept the shape and the name.

The family is large and all of it is round:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{circ}le, \textbf{circ}uit, \textbf{circ}ular, \textbf{circ}umference.
  \item \textbf{circ}a — \textquotedblleft{}around\textquotedblright{} a date.
  \item Spanish \emph{cerca} (\textquotedblleft{}near\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{cercar} (\textquotedblleft{}to surround\textquotedblright{}) come from the same ring.
\end{itemize}

So a circus is not named for clowns or animals. It is named for \textbf{the shape of the floor}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the rule you can see inside one word}]
Most words make you check the letter against the vowel that follows it. \emph{Circo} does the checking for you, because it contains both cases:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{followed by} & \textbf{sound} \\
\midrule
\textbf{c}ir- & i & soft \\
-\textbf{c}o & o & hard \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Keep this word as your reference. Whenever you are unsure how a \textbf{c} should sound, say \emph{circo} and listen to which half matches.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el circo\textquotedblright{} — soft, then hard
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el teatro y el circo\textquotedblright{} — both masculine
  \item what the word is actually named after (the ring — the shape of the floor)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which \textbf{c} in \emph{circo} is soft and why? (The first — it is followed by \textbf{i}.) What does the Latin \emph{circus} mean, and which English words keep it? (A ring: circle, circuit, circa.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cinco lugares]{cinco lugares — five places, sorted by what their names describe}

\label{lesson:ES-C420-repaso-lugares}



\begin{quote}
Name the five places you can now go to. Say them out loud before reading the list.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what each name is actually about}]
Every one of these buildings is named after something different, and once you sort them that way they stop being a list to memorise:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{place} & \textbf{named after} & \textbf{the thing itself} \\
\midrule
el teatro & the audience & a looking-place \\
el cine & the machine & a movement-writer \\
el museo & the Muses & a seat of the arts \\
la exposición & the act & a putting-out \\
el circo & the floor & a ring \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two are named for \textbf{people} (the audience, the Muses), one for a \textbf{machine}, one for an \textbf{action}, and one for a \textbf{shape}. Not one of them is named for the art that happens inside it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four masculine ones with \emph{el} (teatro, cine, museo, circo)
  \item which of the five you would go to in order to \emph{bailar}, and notice that none of them is the obvious answer — the verb needs no place at all
  \item the one feminine one with \emph{la}, and why (\emph{la exposición} — the \textbf{-ción} ending)
  \item which two are named after people (\emph{el teatro}, \emph{el museo})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the five is named after the shape of its floor? (\emph{El circo}.) Which is named after what the audience does? (\emph{El teatro}.) Which one is an event rather than a building? (\emph{La exposición}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[¿Vamos al teatro o al circo?]{¿Vamos al teatro o al circo? — the five places in a real question}

\label{lesson:ES-C420-sintesis-salir}



\begin{quote}
A place you can name is not yet a place you can propose. Ask a friend whether they want to go to the theatre or the circus, out loud, before reading on.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: al and a la, doing the gender work for you}]
Proposing an outing needs \emph{a} (\textquotedblleft{}to\textquotedblright{}) in front of the place, and the article comes along:

\begin{quote}
\emph{¿Vamos \textbf{al} teatro?} — masculine, so \emph{a + el} squeezes into \textbf{al}. \emph{¿Vamos \textbf{a la} exposición?} — feminine, so the two words stay apart.
\end{quote}

Four of your five places take \textbf{al}. Only \emph{la exposición} takes \textbf{a la}, and you can predict which without remembering, because \textbf{-ción} told you the gender when you met the word.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
Every word here is one you have met:

\begin{quote}
—¿Vamos al cine? —No. Vamos al teatro. —¿Y el sábado? —El sábado, a la exposición del museo. Y el domingo, al circo. —¿Y después del circo? —Después, a bailar.
\end{quote}

Four places, one short exchange, and the only thing you had to decide each time was \textbf{al} or \textbf{a la}.

The last line is the exception that proves it. \emph{Bailar} is a verb, not a place, so it takes plain \textbf{a} and no article at all — the same reason \emph{me gusta bailar} needed none.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿Vamos al teatro?\textquotedblright{} — with the opening question mark heard as a rise from the start
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿Vamos a la exposición?\textquotedblright{} — two words, because the noun is feminine
  \item propose the circus, then the museum, in the same shape
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of your five places is the only one that takes \emph{a la}, and how did you know before you had to think about it? (\emph{La exposición} — the \textbf{-ción} ending is feminine.) Say the other four with \emph{al}.
\end{tcolorbox}
